chunks.title: About
chunks.text: As Educational Director and Franchise Director of Anglia Morocco, I’m responsible for developing, administering, and overseeing all educational programs at the Learning Center. I supervise both the full time high school and primary school international American programs, lead curriculum development, testing, and student and staff assessments, and plan staff training, teacher evaluations, and professional development. I manage student recruitment, community outreach, and staff and student relations,

chunks.title: About
chunks.text: as well as the social skills and discipline program. I also actively teach in the classroom. We believe in equality and that an international education empowers students to open global opportunities for their personal growth and success. While we offer a complete education from age five through grade 12, we welcome students at any stage and help them adapt to the AGI curriculum and language immersion process, enabling them to learn English while preserving their native languages. Our diverse program

chunks.title: About
chunks.text: embraces many nationalities, with a focus on student happiness, as we believe a happy child is more likely to succeed. We teach social skills for the whole development of the child and integrate Montessori and Waldorf theories into our American correspondence program. We also offer programs for adults, associations, small groups, and one on one studies, including adult correspondence programs to help learners master English in order to succeed in their chosen fields. Please visit us as we embark

chunks.text: American Group International School Agadir SCHOOL + HOME + COMMUNITY = STUDENT SUCCESS AGIC School in Agadir is a customized private school nestled in the Berber community of Souss Draa in Morocco, North Africa. The first classes of the small school were started in 2013 with five children. In the last 11 years, our program has hosted more than 46+ nationalities. We soon outgrew the one room school so we moved to our location in Nahda, Agadir. Our institution has an open enrollment policy as we are

chunks.title: AGI School – Agadir
chunks.text: a specialized school for students that need special programs that the Moroccan system might not fill. Today American Group International School hosts Kindergarten through 12th grade students and they are taught in eight multi grade classrooms. AGI Philosophy The philosophy of AGI stresses on academic excellence, discipline, ethical standards, and respect for others and for AGI. This philosophy encompasses the intellectual, social, emotional, character, and physical development of students. We want

chunks.title: AGI School – Agadir
chunks.text: students to foster a general respect for all humanity. AGI Vision Since 2013, American Group Internationals faculty and staff have provided students and families with an educational culture best described in our Vision Statement. AGI inspires students to become Inclusive students through language. lifelong learners who pursue excellence, model integrity, and honor cultural diversity. We educate the whole person by equipping minds and building character, empowering students to serve their local community,

chunks.title: Homework Guidelines
chunks.text: Creating a nightly average homework schedule can help ensure students balance their academic responsibilities with other activities. Here’s a suggested schedule by grade levels: Elementary School (Grades K 5) Kindergarten to Grade 1: 10 20 minutes Activities: Reading with parents, simple math exercises, basic writing practice. Grades 2 3: 20 30 minutes Activities: Reading, spelling practice, basic math problems, short writing assignments. Grades 4 5: 30 60 minutes Activities: Reading, spelling/vocabulary

chunks.title: Homework Guidelines
chunks.text: practice, math exercises, small projects, introductory science/social studies tasks. Middle School (Grades 6 8) Grade 6: 60 70 minutes Subjects: Reading, math, science, social studies, language arts. Grade 7: 70 80 minutes Subjects: Reading, math, science, social studies, language arts, introductory foreign language. Grade 8: 80 90 minutes Subjects: Reading, math, science, social studies, language arts, foreign language, project work. High School (Grades 9 12) Grades 9 10: 90 120 minutes Subjects:

chunks.title: Homework Guidelines
chunks.text: English, math, science, social studies, foreign language, electives. Grades 11 12: 120 180 minutes Subjects: English, math, science, social studies, foreign language, advanced placement (AP) or international baccalaureate (IB) courses, college prep activities. Key Considerations: 1. Consistency: Encourage a regular homework routine. 2. Breaks: Integrate short breaks to maintain focus. 3. Prioritization: Start with the most challenging or important assignments. 4. Organization: Use planners or digital

chunks.title: Homework Guidelines
chunks.text: tools to track assignments and deadlines. 5. Balance: Ensure time for extracurricular activities, family, and relaxation. 6. Environment\ \ : Create a quiet, well lit space for homework. Adjustments may be needed based on individual student needs, school requirements, and specific assignments. This schedule serves as a general guideline to help manage and balance students’ academic workloads.

chunks.title: Volunteer Hours
chunks.text: Overview In service volunteer hours are an essential component of the high school experience, providing students with the opportunity to give back to the community, develop leadership skills, and gain real world experience. These hours are also a requirement for graduation at American Group International. Requirements To fulfil the graduation requirement, students must complete a minimum of 40 volunteer hours (10 each year) over the course of their high school career. These hours should be documented

chunks.title: Volunteer Hours
chunks.text: and approved by the school. Eligible Activities Volunteer activities should: Benefit the community or an organization. Be unpaid and voluntary. Not be part of a regular job or family obligation. Be approved by the school coordinator in advance if the organization is not on the pre approved list. Examples of Eligible Activities: Volunteering at local non profits (soup kitchens, shelters, etc.). Participating in community clean up projects. Assisting in local libraries or museums. Helping at school

chunks.title: Volunteer Hours
chunks.text: events outside regular school hours. Tutoring or mentoring younger students. Involvement in faith based service projects (if open to the wider community). Non Eligible Activities: Tasks that are part of a paid job. Family chores or personal family business. Activities without prior approval from the volunteer coordinator. Court ordered community service. Documentation and Approval Process 1. Pre Approval: Before starting a new volunteer activity, students should seek preapproval from the volunteer

chunks.title: Volunteer Hours
chunks.text: coordinator if the organization is not on the pre approved list. 2. Log Hours: Students must maintain a volunteer log to document their hours. This log should include: Date of service Grades 9, 10, 11, 12. Description of the activity Number of hours completed Supervisor's name and contact information Supervisor's signature 1. Submission: Completed volunteer logs should be submitted to the volunteer coordinator by [Specific Deadlines], usually at the end of each semester. 2. Verification: The volunteer

chunks.title: Volunteer Hours
chunks.text: coordinator will verify the hours with the organization or supervisor listed on the log. 3. Approval: Once verified, hours will be recorded in the student's file towards their graduation requirement. Benefits of Volunteering Skill Development: Gain skills in leadership, teamwork, and problem solving. Career Exploration: Explore potential career interests and gain experience. College Applications: Enhance college applications and resumes with documented community service. Personal Growth: Build self

chunks.title: Volunteer Hours
chunks.text: esteem, compassion, and a sense of responsibility.

chunks.title: ADHD Holistic Coaching
chunks.text: Holistic Practitioners offer a comprehensive, non medical approach to managing Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) by using natural and supportive strategies to address the underlying symptoms. Their work focuses on enhancing an individual's overall well being and empowering them to manage ADHD effectively in various aspects of life. Here’s a breakdown of what ADHD Holistic Practitioners do: 1. Individualized Coaching: Holistic practitioners offer personalized coaching, working closely

chunks.title: ADHD Holistic Coaching
chunks.text: with clients to understand their specific challenges. They create customized strategies and plans to help individuals manage ADHD symptoms, such as inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. 2. Behavioral and Cognitive Strategies: Practitioners help individuals develop skills to regulate emotions, improve focus, and enhance organizational abilities. This includes teaching practical strategies like time management, task prioritization, and setting achievable goals. 3. Diet and Nutrition Guidance:

chunks.title: ADHD Holistic Coaching
chunks.text: A significant part of holistic therapy involves addressing diet and nutrition. ADHD Holistic Practitioners often recommend dietary changes, emphasizing foods that support brain health and emotional regulation. They might suggest eliminating processed foods or additives and incorporating more whole foods, essential fatty acids, and micronutrients to enhance cognitive function and emotional balance. 4. Exercise and Physical Activity: Exercise is a key component in managing ADHD symptoms. Holistic practitioners

chunks.title: ADHD Holistic Coaching
chunks.text: encourage physical activities that help improve focus, release excess energy, and reduce anxiety. Regular exercise, like walking, yoga, or sports, is incorporated into a treatment plan to boost overall health and mental clarity. 5. Play Therapy (for Children): For children with ADHD, play therapy is often used to help them express emotions, develop social skills, and improve focus in a non threatening, fun environment. It encourages creativity and self expression while providing a structured way

chunks.title: ADHD Holistic Coaching
chunks.text: for children to work through their challenges. 6. Mindfulness and Stress Management Techniques: Holistic practitioners often incorporate mindfulness, meditation, and relaxation techniques into their coaching sessions. These practices help reduce stress, improve concentration, and enhance emotional regulation. Mindfulness helps individuals with ADHD to stay grounded and become more aware of their thoughts and behaviors in the present moment. 7. Support in Developing Routines and Time Management: Creating

chunks.title: ADHD Holistic Coaching
chunks.text: a structured routine is critical for individuals with ADHD. Holistic practitioners help clients—especially children—develop time management skills, build schedules, and learn how to stick to a routine. This structure helps reduce anxiety, improves focus, and allows individuals to manage their day more effectively. 8. Family Support and Education: Holistic practitioners also work with families to provide support and education on ADHD. They teach families how to best support the individual, offer coping

chunks.title: ADHD Holistic Coaching
chunks.text: mechanisms, and help set realistic expectations. By taking a holistic, individualized approach, ADHD Holistic Practitioners aim to not only alleviate the symptoms of ADHD but also help individuals thrive by improving their overall quality of life through sustainable lifestyle changes, emotional well being, and practical skills development. chunks.text: GET YOUR TESOL WITH US! CITE with Anglia Examinations About the C.I.T.E Exams: Exams for Teachers of English TESOL. C.I.T.E. is Anglia Examinations' Certificate for International Teachers of English. These exams provide teacher certification for English teachers, who may or may not have any other English teaching qualifications, and gives them an opportunity to obtain recognition for their English language teaching skills, knowledge and experience. Our C.I.T.E. exams work on the same principle as

chunks.title: C.I.T.E Teacher Training
chunks.text: any other test of English for special purposes. In this case the special purpose is teaching English. The tests are mapped to the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) and our C.I.T.E certificate provides evidence of English teaching ability. Who is C.I.T.E. for? There are no entry qualifications for the C.I.T.E. test. Although you may well have previous qualifications in English, none are compulsory requirements. The C.I.T.E. test is not in itself a teaching qualification,

chunks.title: C.I.T.E Teacher Training
chunks.text: but recognition of your competence in the relevant English language skills needed for teaching. It can, therefore, equally be taken by teachers who are currently teaching English, or students who are planning to, and have gained knowledge of classroom language and practice through study. It may, for example, be taken by High School mathematics teachers who find themselves timetabled with two lessons of English a week, by Primary school teachers who have been co opted into teaching English under a

chunks.title: C.I.T.E Teacher Training
chunks.text: government initiative, or English teachers whose original qualification concentrated on 19th Century literature and who want to have a focus for updating their practical, classroom language skills. The C.I.T.E. tests recognise that teaching young learners and teaching higher level, older, learners may require different language levels, theory and practice. For this reason, candidates are offered three versions of the test: C.I.T.E. C.I.T.E. (Young Learners) C.I.T.E. (Very Young Learners). Referring

chunks.title: C.I.T.E Teacher Training
chunks.text: to a sample paper should help a candidate or their representative decide which level is the most appropriate. Primary school teachers are not obliged to take either of the Young Learner versions, but the opportunity is available. What level of English do you need? You need the level of English required to be a competent teacher. If you think you have this, it is likely that you are at the right level for the C.I.T.E. test. For the C.I.T.E. it is likely that your level of English will be C1 on the

chunks.title: C.I.T.E Teacher Training
chunks.text: CEFR. For the C.I.T.E. (YL) your level of English should be at least B2 on the CEFR. For the C.I.T.E. (VYL) your level of English should be at least B1 on the CEFR. It isn't easy to relate the level required to any general English test. However, the English required in the C.I.T.E. tests is related to knowledge of grammatical terms and functions in English included in the main suite syllabus, together with classroom language in English. Although your representative may be able to indicate where you can find a suitable local course or study group, there is no set course either in English or in teaching which leads to the C.I.T.E. test. chunks.title: Business Examinations
chunks.text: Anglia Exams offers a range of Business English Exams that test the English proficiency level of students whose special interest is business. The exams are divided into four steps, ranging in level from A2+ to C1 on the CEFR, and test all four skills of reading, writing, listening and speaking. The exams are designed to evaluate the linguistic competence of candidates who may be considering a future in an international workplace or may already be working in the professional world1. If you’re interested

chunks.title: Business Examinations
chunks.text: in taking one of these exams, you can visit Anglia Exams for more information. Business English Exams English is the lingua franca of business. No matter where in the world you live or work, the ability to communicate effectively in English is a definite advantage when conducting business. In an increasingly globalised world, being proficient in business English gives you a competitive edge. The four steps of the Anglia Business English exams, ranging in level from A2+ to C1 on the CEFR, test the

chunks.title: Business Examinations
chunks.text: English proficiency level of students whose special interest is business. Candidates may be considering a future in an international workplace or may already be working in the professional world and be keen to evaluate their linguistic competence. With an emphasis on practical business application in realistic situations, our communicative exams offer a progressive choice of levels: A2+, B1, B2 and C1, and test all four skills of reading, writing, listening and speaking.

chunks.title: AIM Accreditation
chunks.text: Regulated by Ofqual AIM Qualifications and Assessment Group (AIM Qualifications) is an awarding organization in the UK that offers a wide range of qualifications and assessments. They are recognized for providing innovative and flexible qualifications across various sectors, including vocational qualifications, end point assessments, and bespoke qualifications for employers. chunks.text: such as business, health and social care, sport, and more. They offer qualifications from entry level to higher levels, catering to a diverse range of learners. 2. Assessment Approach: AIM Qualifications emphasizes flexibility and innovation in their assessment methods, ensuring they meet the needs of learners and employers. Affiliation with Anglia Examinations England: 1. Partnership: AIM Qualifications collaborates with Anglia Examinations England, which is known for its English language assessments.

chunks.title: AIM Accreditation
chunks.text: This partnership allows both organizations to leverage their expertise and resources to offer comprehensive educational solutions. 2. English Language Qualifications: Through this affiliation, AIM Qualifications supports the delivery and recognition of Anglia's English language qualifications, ensuring they meet high standards and are widely recognized. UK Recognition and Support: 1. Regulatory Approval: AIM Qualifications is regulated by Ofqual (Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulation),

chunks.title: AIM Accreditation
chunks.text: which is the regulatory body for qualifications, exams, and assessments in England. This ensures that their qualifications meet national standards for quality and rigor. 2. Recognition by Educational Institutions and Employers: Qualifications awarded by AIM are recognized by educational institutions and employers across the UK, providing learners with valuable credentials that can support their educational and career advancement. 3. Support from UK Education System: The recognition and regulation

chunks.title: AIM Accreditation
chunks.text: by Ofqual signify that AIM Qualifications are supported by the UK education system. This support is crucial for maintaining the credibility and acceptance of the qualifications both nationally and internationally. Conclusion: AIM Qualifications Group plays a significant role in the UK education sector by offering a variety of qualifications and assessments. Their affiliation with Anglia Examinations England enhances the reach and recognition of English language qualifications. The regulatory oversight

chunks.title: AIM Accreditation
chunks.text: by Ofqual ensures that their qualifications are held to high standards, thereby receiving support and recognition from educational institutions and employers within the UK. The Office of Qualifications & Examinations Regulation (Ofqual) Ofqual regulate qualifications, examinations and assessments in England. Ofqual are independent of government and report directly to Parliament. Ofqual's responsibilities are to provide confidence in the qualifications they regulate and indicate the knowledge, skills

chunks.title: AIM Accreditation
chunks.text: and understanding students have demonstrated. Ofqual maintain standards and provide confidence in the rigour of qualifications in England including GCSEs, A levels, AS levels and vocational and technical qualifications, including AIM Qualifications and Assessment Group. Anglia Examinations top four levels of English language exams are regulated by Ofqual via our partnership with AIM Qualifications and Assessment Group. chunks.title: Medical EFL
chunks.text: No matter your specialty, as a medical professional your foremost concern should always be the tongue. It is the tongue – and the language that is generated by it – that allows health providers to communicate with patients and medical colleagues, speak at seminars and medical meetings – ultimately – how to read and write medical papers. Though patients – and their mother tongues – come in all different shapes and sizes, more and more it is English that is on the tips of the tongues of patients around

chunks.title: Medical EFL
chunks.text: the world. That is because even though in today’s increasingly globalized world a doctor’s patients may speak many different languages, the special status that English enjoys as the 21st Century’s lingua franca means that it is increasingly called upon to unite doctor and patient in examining rooms around the world. After all, in addition to the 500 million people worldwide who speak English natively, more than a billion more – or all together a quarter of the world’s population – speak it as a second

chunks.title: Medical EFL
chunks.text: language. Thus the role of English in medicine cannot be overstated. So whether you are working in an English speaking country or even in your own home country, there will come a time when you will need to rely on English to communicate. All this, then, explains why it is important to learn medical English. In so doing, medical professionals of all types – be they general practice physicians, specialists, nurses, pharmacists, paramedics, and even medical volunteers – will be able to meet the needs

chunks.title: Medical EFL
chunks.text: of their patients, be better equipped to console the loved ones of their patients, and be better prepared to communicate with other medical professionals who speak English. Given the obvious advantages, it is easier to understand why you learn medical English than it is to understand exactly how. Fortunately, a growing number of English language programs are offered throughout the English speaking world to meet the needs of aspiring medical professionals. Be forewarned, however: such medical English

chunks.title: Medical EFL
chunks.text: courses are not like normal intensive English programs. As specialized programs, designed to foster the ability to communicate in English in a hospital or clinical setting, students should already have mastery of general (conversational) English at an intermediate or advanced level and be ready to add to their working knowledge of the language. In much the same way, because the focus is on language and not science, students should have an understanding of anatomy, physiology, and indeed of their

chunks.title: Medical EFL
chunks.text: medical concentration in general in their native language, as well. Students will be best able to learn medical English by using a strong foundation in both conversational English and medical science as a springboard for success. Though courses may vary depending on the provider, when it comes time to choose a medical English course, there are certain things to look for. A quality program, for example, will help international students comes to terms with the intricacies of medical terminology in

chunks.title: Medical EFL
chunks.text: areas as diverse as history taking, trauma care, and treatment procedures. In addition to a focus on industry specific vocabulary, good programs should highlight commonly used grammatical structures used in the field of medicine and help candidates master the kind of medical idioms that are at the heart of doctor to doctor and doctor to patient interaction. Finally, with an eye on advancement, comprehensive may even provide modules that explain the inner workings of the U.S. healthcare system and

chunks.title: Medical EFL
chunks.text: contribute to the growth of medical writing skills. Upon completion of such a course, providers should feel comfortable working not just on tongue but in the English tongue. After all, as both working and aspiring medical professionals both know, no matter our mother tongue, all tongues themselves are the same and deserving of the same standard of care.

chunks.text: Printable Nursery Rhymes Booklet Nursery Rhymes Songs Fingerplays Printable Cards Rhymes and Songs for Babies and Toddlers Rhymes and songs provide a wonderful way for you to bond with your child. Your child will love being able to spend time with you in this way. Saying rhymes and singing songs is fun! Your child is naturally drawn to the beat, and you might be impressed to see how well your child bounces or dances to the rhythm of a favorite song or rhyme. Rhymes and songs are great tools for helping

chunks.title: Nursery Rhymes Pre-K
chunks.text: your child explore the fun and beauty of language. The rhythm that your child naturally finds so appealing also helps your child to hear all of the individual sounds that make up the words. This is important for helping children learn to speak when they are very young. As they grow older, it will help them learn to read on their own. Rhymes and songs allow your child to experience language with many senses. For example, your child may enjoy a rhyme with his/her ears (hearing), body (moving or bouncing),

chunks.title: Nursery Rhymes Pre-K
chunks.text: and/or with touch (tickles) all at the same time. The more senses a child uses, the stronger the activity’s impact will be. The old system of indicating the pronunciation by numerals, called

The Revised Speller conforms in orthography, pronunciation, and syllabication to the latest edition of Webster's Unabridged Diction­ary. Exercises have been given on each of the distinctive marks used in the book, as will be seen by reference to Lessons 36 57. In arranging the text of the several lessons, the object has been not to appeal merely to arbitrary memory, but to asso­ciate each lesson with some principle of sound, meaning, or accent, which would tend to aid the pupil in acquiring a knowledge of our language. Several distinct lessons on pro­nunciation are given, and towards the close of the book numerous lessons of difficult words in orthography have been introduced. Instead of indicating silent letters

D., who planned and executed this revision. DECEMBER, 1879. 16 Copyright, 1879, by Van Antwerp, Bragg & Co. (ii) THE ENGLISH ALPHABET. The English Alphabet

chunks.title: McGuffey's Sight Words
chunks.text: consists of twenty six letters, viz.: a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h,i,j,k,l,m,n,o,p,q,r,s,t,u,v,w,x,y,z. Letters are divided into VOWELS and CONSONANTS. The Vowels are those letters which can be perfectly sounded without the aid of any other letter. The vowels are a, e, i, o, u, w , and y. The vowel sounds of w and y are the same as those of u and i . A, e , and o are always vowels. I, u, w , and y are sometimes consonants. A Diphthong is the union of two vowels in one sound. When both vowels are sounded, the

chunks.title: McGuffey's Sight Words
chunks.text: diphthong is called PROPER, because then it is really a DIPHTHONG, or double sound; that is, the sounds of the vowels unite; as, oi in oil ; ou in sound . When only one of the vowels is sounded, the diphthong is called IMPROPER, because then, as one of the vowels is silent, it is not properly a DIPHTHONG, though it takes that name; as, oa in boat , ui in suit , where a and i are silent. The following diphthongs are in common use, viz.: oi, oy, ou, ow, ae, ai, au, aw, ay, ea, ei, eo, eu, ew, ey, ia,

chunks.title: McGuffey's Sight Words
chunks.text: ie, oa, oe, ua, ue, ui ; as in toil, boy, round, plow, seal, coal, head, sail, say, aught, yeoman . Of these, oi, oy, ou , and ow are gener­ally proper diphthongs; though sometimes ou and ow are improper, as in famous , where o is silent, and in slow , where w is silent. A Triphthong is the union of three vowels in one syllable; as, eau in beau , iew in view . The triphthong is properly a union of letters , not sounds . (iii) 4 ECLECTIC SERIES. OF THE VARIOUS SOUNDS. chunks.title: McGuffey's Sight Words
chunks.text: consonants are b, c, d, f, g, h, l, k, l, m, n, p, q, r, s, t, v, x, z, and sometimes i, u, w, and y . The consonants are divided into MUTES and SEMI VOWELS . The u is canceled in this book when qu is sounded like k . 6 ECLECTIC SERIES. The Semi vowels are those consonants that can be sounded imperfectly by themselves. chunks.title: McGuffey's Sight Words

OF SYLLABLES AND WORDS. A Syllable is a sound, or a combination of sounds, uttered by a single impulse of the voice: it may have one or more letters; as a, bad, bad ness. A Word is either a syllable or a combination of syllables; as, not, notion . A word of one syllable is called a Monosyllable ; as, man . A word of two syllables

chunks.title: McGuffey's Sight Words
chunks.text: is called a Dissyllable ; as, manly . A word of three syllables is called a Trisyllable ; as, manliness. Words of more than three syllables are called Polysyllables . Accent is a stress of voice placed upon some one sylla­ble more than the others. Every word composed of two or more syllables has one of them accented. This accent is denoted by a mark (') at the end of the accented syllable; as, mid'night , a ban'don . A Primitive Word is one which is not derived from any other word; as, man, great,

chunks.title: McGuffey's Sight Words
chunks.text: full. A Derivative Word is one which is formed from some other word by adding something to it; as, manful, greatness, fully . A Simple Word is one which is not composed of more than one word; as, kind, man, stand, ink . A Compound Word is one that is composed of two or more simple words; as, ink stand, wind mill. chunks.title: McGuffey's Sight Words
chunks.text: 144 ECLECTIC SERIES. Lesson 248. OF CHARACTERS USED IN PUNCTUATION. A Comma [, ] denotes the slightest degree of separation be­tween the elements of a sentence. A Semicolon [; ] denotes a degree of separation somewhat greater than that indicated by a comma. A Colon [:] marks a still greater degree of separation than a semicolon. A Period [.] usually indicates the close of a sentence. The Interrogation Point [?] is used at the end of a ques­tion. The Exclamation Point [!] denotes astonishment or other

chunks.title: McGuffey's Sight Words
chunks.text: emotion. A Hyphen [ ] is used to join words or syllables. A Dash [ ] marks a sudden break or stop in a sentence. A Parenthesis [( )] includes words which might be left out without injuring the sense. Brackets [ ] inclose words, etc., intended to explain or rec­tify what precedes or follows. An Apostrophe ['] indicates the omission of one or more letters; or denotes the possessive case. Quotation Marks [" "] show that the passage included, is taken from some other author. OF CAPITAL LETTERS. A Capital

PEDAGOGY/THEORY OF THE NORTH AMERICAN EDUCATIONAL SYSTEM— In the North American education system, students are the first priority; they are partners in the educational experience. Student thinking is valued even when it is flawed, with their errors used as opportunities for educational growth.

chunks.title: Academic Handbook
chunks.text: Teachers, while respected, are not viewed as fully informed experts who transmit their knowledge, but as professionals who facilitate and model cooperative learning. North American education emphasizes learning experiences in which children actively participate, learning by hands on work and experimentation, solving problems that are real and important to them. The learning process utilizes interactive instruction methods such as discussions, debates, teamwork activities, and community service projects

chunks.title: Academic Handbook
chunks.text: to elicit imaginative thinking, problem solving and decision making toward a goal of meaningful insight. Learning how to learn is key to the students’ ultimate success in life, and the North American education system places great importance on this principle. ACADEMICS PLAGIARISM Plagiarism occurs when a student presents another person’s work as

chunks.title: Academic Handbook
chunks.text: his or her own. This includes copying in part or whole from any source, without acknowledgment of authorship. Plagiarizing someone else’s ideas is perceived as stealing their intellectual property. Whether it is intentional or not, it is taken as a serious matter in any educational institution. To avoid plagiarism, make sure you acknowledge the source of any material you use which belongs to someone else. Your teachers will show you how to do this. As a guide, follow these three rules: Exact words

chunks.title: Academic Handbook
chunks.text: from a source must be put in quotation marks and the source acknowledged. Even if you reword a passage, you must give credit to the source. Even if you summarize a passage, you must give credit to the source. The intention is to acknowledge your use of ideas originating with someone else. The penalty for plagiarism at AGI is a mark of O (zero) for the offending assignment and possible referral to Administration for further disciplinary action, including possible Academic Probation or Suspension.

chunks.title: Academic Handbook

Cheating also involves violating the rules set down for the task by the teacher and the AGI Behaviour Expectations. The penalty for cheating is a zero mark for the task, and possible referral to the Administration for further disciplinary action, including

chunks.title: Attendance Policy
chunks.text: American Group International of Agadir, Morocco shall maintain a strict attendance policy that adheres to students’ best interests as well as the law. As a qualification for promotion to the next grade level in grades K 12, students must be in attendance 90% of the year. In accordance with State laws, parents must provide a dated and signed excuse stating the reason for any absence. The excuse must be submitted no later than two days after the student returns to school. A student who arrives at school

chunks.title: Attendance Policy
chunks.text: after 10:00 a.m. is considered absent for the full day. A student is considered late and will be marked on school records as such if he/she arrives after 9:00 a.m. Furthermore, if a student has (5) unexcused tardies past 9:00 am, that equates to one (1) unexcused day absent. Students have the right to make up assignments missed during any excused absence. Parents and students have the right to review school policies which clearly define what is considered an excused absence, an unexcused absence,

chunks.title: Attendance Policy
chunks.text: and tardiness. Parents and students also have the right to appeal a decision concerning whether an absence is excused or unexcused. Tardiness: When a child reports late, they must obtain a late slip from the front desk (whether he/she is arriving to school late or has arrived at school early but is late getting to the classroom). The admin office shall be responsible for recording the student’s name, date, time, and reason for tardiness on a Late Slip designed for that purpose. After recording the

chunks.title: Attendance Policy
chunks.text: information, the receptionist shall give the student that slip to give to the teacher. Teachers will mark tardiness or absence on the student record . Students arriving to school after 9:00 must provide the office with a written note from the parent stating the reason the student is late or “absent”. Once the note is received the student will be given a late slip to be admitted to the classroom. If a student does not have an acceptable reason for being tardy, he/she will be marked unexcused tardy.

chunks.title: Attendance Policy
chunks.text: Arrival after 10:00 a.m.: Students arriving after 10:00 a.m. are considered and remain marked as “absent” for the full day. Parents should make every effort to have their children well rested, fed and in school on time daily. Absences: Students who are absent must return to school with a note from a parent/guardian. A student absent for three or more days due to illness must have a signed excuse from their doctor upon returning to school. Students who are absent or sent home because they contracted

chunks.title: Attendance Policy
chunks.text: a communicable disease such as COVID 19, pinkeye, head lice, ringworm, chicken pox, etc. must be seen by a physician and provide a doctor’s note indicating they can return to school. The admin office shall keep all parents notes or doctors’ excuses in the student file. Notes that state long term absences from school, i.e., vacation, extended family trip, are not counted as excused; hence, parents are encouraged to plan voluntary, non emergency extended absences around the school calendar. Acceptable

chunks.title: Attendance Policy

chunks.text: Promotion and Retention Procedures Policy Promotion from one grade to another normally occurs at the end of the school year. Students are allowed to the next grade by completing grade level criteria set up by the curriculum. The following criteria will be used to decide the student’s placement into the next grade or retention in the current grade: Promotion • The student’s understanding of current grade level curriculum in all the following subjects: • Math, Science, Language Arts and Social Studies.

chunks.title: Promotion & Retention
chunks.text: • Students must pass each core subject with at least a 64% (D) or above to be considered as “passing.” • The student’s attendance record (90% of enrolled days) • The student’s maturity level is proven throughout the year. • English Assessment Testing for guaranteed levels completed. Retention • Student’s inability to receive a 64% or above in two or more of the subject areas above. • Poor attendance • Immaturity; and, • Consensus of teacher and Principal. • Students who have not met the above promotion

chunks.title: Promotion & Retention
chunks.text: requirements will not be promoted into the next grade. Students who have not met the attendance requirement due to excused illness or injury will be promoted supplied their grades are adequate. • Students who have been kept may attend summer remediation to see if the grade level aims can be met. Once they have successfully completed this remediation, they will need to be retested at AGI to figure out if they can pass the course of study. By enrolling, parents/guardians agree to follow these terms to ensure a safe, structured, and effective learning environment. 1. First 90 Day Adjustment Period The first 90 days of enrollment are an adjustment period. Students must attend regularly, participate, and complete assigned work. Concerns must be addressed early. After this period, late concerns may not result in

chunks.title: Parent Policy

The school cannot evaluate academic level accurately without consistent attendance and work completion. 3. Learning Difficulties & Documentation If a learning difficulty is suspected,

Academic Placement Testing If a student is placed incorrectly, the school may conduct assessments in subjects such as Math or English. Late year changes are not guaranteed. 7. Program

chunks.title: Placement & Assessment
chunks.text: Purpose: This policy ensures that all new students admitted to American Group International (AGI) are placed appropriately in their grade and academic tracks, even when prior school documentation is missing or incomplete. It reflects AGI’s commitment to inclusive education, student safety, and the academic success of every student. 1. Mandatory Assessment for All New Students All students entering AGI for the first time, whether from a French system, English system, or any other educational system,

chunks.title: Placement & Assessment
chunks.text: must complete assessment tests before admission. Required assessments include: English / ESL proficiency Anglia Examinations Assessment Level Mathematics (CAT) Language Arts / Reading (CAT) Other core academic subjects if needed Placement into academic tracks will be determined based on these assessments, even if prior school records are provided. Normally we let children in the grade placement for their age. 2. Provisional Admission Students may be admitted provisionally if: Required prior school

chunks.title: Placement & Assessment
chunks.text: documentation (transcripts, report cards, assessment results) is missing. Provisional admission is temporary, valid for a maximum of 60 calendar days from the student’s first day of school. During this period, the student’s grade placement and academic support will be determined using internal assessments. 3. Placement Decisions (Inclusive Education Approach) Grade Placement: Students are kept in the grade they enter, consistent with AGI’s commitment to inclusive education. Grade placement is not

chunks.title: Placement & Assessment
chunks.text: lowered due to missing documents, language gaps, or academic gaps. Academic Support: Students who are behind in specific subjects will receive targeted support to help them reach grade level expectations. Support may include: ESL classes Simplified or scaffolded materials Additional tutoring or guided practice Progress is monitored regularly, and support is adjusted as the student improves. Provisional Placement Exceptions: In rare cases where a student demonstrates severe gaps that prevent participation

chunks.title: Placement & Assessment
chunks.text: at grade level, temporary adjustments may be made with administrative approval. 4. Documentation Follow Up Parents/guardians must provide all prior academic records within 60 calendar days of the student’s first day of school. It is the parents’ responsibility to submit documentation. The school is not required to repeatedly request missing records. After 60 calendar days, if records are not provided, the school will determine grade placement and academic support based on internal assessments and

chunks.title: Placement & Assessment
chunks.text: the student’s performance. All communications with parents regarding the initial request for documentation must be logged by the administration office. 5. Support for Students with Academic Gaps Students identified as behind in English, math, or other subjects will receive: Supplemental instruction Simplified or scaffolded curriculum materials Targeted ESL support Progress will be monitored regularly to ensure the student reaches grade level expectations. 6. Transparency and Compliance Parental Responsibility:

chunks.title: Placement & Assessment
chunks.text: Parents/guardians must provide complete and accurate information regarding their child’s: Learning differences or disabilities (e.g., ADHD, dyslexia) Special needs Medical or psychological conditions relevant to schooling Reports from doctors, therapists, or specialists School Review and parental dishonesty: If it is discovered that critical information has been intentionally withheld, the school administration will: Conduct a review meeting with relevant administrative staff. Evaluate the student’s

chunks.title: Placement & Assessment
chunks.text: needs, safety, and the school’s ability to provide appropriate support. Administrative Action: Based on the review, the school reserves the right to dismiss a student if parents are not complying with disclosure requirements. The decision to dismiss is not a reflection on the student, but a measure to ensure: Proper educational support Safety and well being of the student and other students Compliance with school rules and policies. Documentation: All meetings, decisions, and communications regarding

chunks.title: Placement & Assessment
chunks.text: withheld information will be documented in the student’s file. 7. Responsibilities Role Responsibility Principal / Academic Director Approves provisional placement, oversees assessment administration, ensures students receive necessary support. Teachers Conduct assessments, document results, provide modified instruction, report progress. Administration Office Maintains communication with parents, logs all requests for missing documentation, tracks 60 day deadlines. 8. Policy Review This policy is

chunks.title: Placement & Assessment
chunks.text: reviewed annually and updated as needed to align with best practices in international education and accreditation standards. Approved by: Julie Wilburn, Director American Group International Policy 2026

Some images may be used in printed materials,

chunks.title: Media Policy

chunks.title: Tutoring Session Length
chunks.text: Depending on who you ask, the word “tutoring” could mean a multitude of things. For some, it’s a quick bit of homework help. For others, it’s an every other day support system and confidence booster. If you’re just getting started with tutoring, it’s tough to figure out which approach is best. So, how long should a tutoring session last, and how many sessions should you schedule? It’s no wonder why this is one oof our frequently asked questions!To put it plainly, it depends. Every student is different

chunks.title: Tutoring Session Length
chunks.text: and has different needs. For those with a greater attention span, you can get away with longer sessions. Longer is not always better though, and some students get more value out of shorter sessions. Based on Age, How Long Should Tutoring Sessions Be? When kids are younger, they tend to get distracted more easily. Asking them to sit down for any period feels like a lot, so shorter sessions suit them better. Conversely, older students can usually handle working for longer periods of time. A tutoring

chunks.title: Tutoring Session Length
chunks.text: session should be no shorter than 45 minutes . Less than that isn’t enough time for students to gain new information and internalize it. This is especially true if tutoring is only happening once a week. If your student can’t stay focused for more than 45 minutes, consider having tutoring sessions twice per week. As your child gets older, you can stretch the tutoring sessions to get more accomplished in a day. This is great if you have a busy schedule because you can have one fully dedicated tutoring

chunks.title: Tutoring Session Length
chunks.text: day each week. It’s not unheard of to have a three hour tutoring session, but two hours is usually a good upper limit. Extending it too long can sometimes do more harm than good. For a general guideline, we’ve created an age based chart to help you get started. Grade Level Session Length Sessions Per Week K to 5 45 minutes to 1 hour 1 to 2 6 to 9 1 to 1.5 hours 1 to 3 10 to 12 1 to 2 hours 1 to 3 Traditional Schooling vs Homeschooling The nature of tutoring will vary depending on whether your child

chunks.title: Tutoring Session Length
chunks.text: is attending brick and mortar school. Make sure you take this into account when scheduling your tutoring sessions. Should they be online or in person. Traditional Schooling Students attending traditional school can greatly benefit from the extra support a tutor provides. A one hour session once per week is a solid start, but you might want to supplement that with an additional session for best results. Homeschooling If you’re homeschooling your child, especially if they’re in high school, you’ll

chunks.title: Tutoring Session Length
chunks.text: want to provide more tutoring time. Consider scheduling at least two sessions per week , both anywhere from one to two hours each . This will ensure that your student receives the assistance they need. Tutors can function as teachers, so you can ask them to teach your child’s curriculum. Make sure you allocate enough time to accomplish the goals you would like your tutor to achieve. To simulate a school environment, you can experiment with longer sessions divided by short breaks to improve engagement.

chunks.title: Tutoring Session Length
chunks.text: Two hour or even three hour sessions work well in this case. Choose a Productive Time of Day It’s important to determine how long a tutoring session should last, but you want to make sure the session is during a productive time of day. Conducting a session too late could lead to your child fatiguing and losing interest. If the session is too early, they might not be fully awake yet. Tutoring sessions immediately after school tend to be quite effective. The child will not have settled into the away

chunks.title: Tutoring Session Length
chunks.text: from school mindset just yet, leading to higher levels of focus. If you’re homeschooling, sessions in the late morning and early afternoon can maximize your child’s accomplishments. These are peak hours for productivity, giving your student a head start on success. Ask Your Child How Long Should a Tutoring Session Last Ultimately, your child is the one receiving the tutoring, so they should have a say in the matter. Check in with them to see what they would like and use that information to plan accordingly.

chunks.title: Tutoring Session Length
chunks.text: Also, try different times of day to see what works best for them. Consult Your Tutor Your tutor will get to know your child quite well, and they’ll be able to provide useful information about your child’s habits. Ask for progress reports to see if anything can be adjusted. They’ll let you know if they’re spending too much time trying to keep a lid on things during a long session or if they often wish for more time during shorter ones. Communication is key! We Can Help You Decide How Long a Tutoring

chunks.title: Tutoring Session Length
chunks.text: Session Should Last We know tutoring is a big commitment with a ton of variables, so we’re here to support you. Tutoring…With a Twist\ will create a specialized plan that works for you. We’ll guide you through every step of the way and come up with a perfect tutoring schedule for your child. If you’re ready to get started, don’t hesitate to contact us! (agiangliama@gmail.com). We’d love to hear from you! Thank you for your interest in our Tutor’s.

chunks.title: Online Classes for Language Students starting in June 2020.
chunks.text: What is an online/virtual classroom??? A virtual classroom is a digital replica of a traditional classroom or training room. The instructors teach, and the participants learn in real time, face to face but via internet enabled technology devices. The classroom or the meeting room staple – whiteboard – remains intact. Brainstorming, idealization, and discussions happen in real time. Tests are given and taken pre and post the session. The reports are ready right after the session is over. Everything remains the way it is. The only difference is: an online classroom uses technology to support instruction and learning. What are the advantages of a virtual classroom? It offers more flexibility over a traditional classroom. You can deliver the instruction to a geographically dispersed audience at one time. Both the instructors and learners have rich experience of collaborating with other learners and instructors from around the world. The attendance is automatically tracked. Moreover, online collaboration typically incorporates more communication tools, such as chat, open discussion boards, polls, multimedia content, and social media.
